item.title: BEHIND THE NEWS I Youth development, a shared commitment
item.description: IN Fiji’s highlands, geography can mean more than distance — it can shape how young people access health information, education, employment and other opportunities. item.content:encoded:
IN Fiji’s highlands, geography can mean more than distance — it can shape how young people access health information, education, employment and other opportunities.

United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) technical specialist for Adolescents and Youth, Dr Tej Ram Jat, said where a young person lives should never become a barrier to the information and services, they need to live healthy, empowered and dignified lives.

Speaking at the youth festival in Navosa last week, Dr Jat said holding the festival in Navosa demonstrated a commitment to reaching young people wherever they live.

“It represents our shared commitment for ensuring that young people, youth development, their health, their empowerment, reach every young person in Fiji, no matter where they live, whether they live in Suva, in Lautoka, Ba or in the highlands of Navosa,” he said.

Dr Jat extended the United Nations’ congratulations to the Ministry of Youth and Sports for hosting the event, saying the gathering reflected the aspirations young people share despite living in different circumstances.

The message reflected this year’s International Youth Day theme, “Different Contexts, Common Aspirations.”

Navosa gave the theme particular meaning, Dr Jat said, as young people from different communities and backgrounds, including agricultural communities, gathered for the festival.

Their geographic circumstances may affect access to health services, education and employment opportunities, but those differences do not change their hopes for the future.

“They all share common aspirations,” he said.

Those aspirations include living healthy and dignified lives, making informed choices about their bodies, health and wellbeing, and accessing quality information and services.

Dr Jat said young people’s ambitions also extend beyond their individual lives.

He pointed to the Pacific youth-led global campaign on climate change, which resulted in an International Court of Justice advisory, as an example of young people taking action on issues affecting their communities, countries and the wider world.

He said the achievement demonstrated the strength and initiative of young people in Fiji and across the Pacific.

“It shows how young people from the Pacific, from Fiji and other Pacific nations, are vibrant, how they are strong, how they are proactive, how they make informed decisions about their lives,” he said.

Almost 44 per cent of Fiji’s population is below the age of 25.

These young people live in urban areas, rural communities and the highlands, but wherever they live, they are the backbone of a sustainable and resilient future for Fiji.

“So this demographic profile offers Fiji a wonderful opportunity to realise the benefits of demographic dividend.

“And the demographic dividend is a situation where we have young people in the workforce who are skilled, who are educated, who are healthy, and who make very significant contribution in sustainable socioeconomic development of the country.”

But that opportunity depends on investment.

“We will be able to achieve only if we are investing appropriately in health, education, skills development and wellbeing of these young people, which they deserve,” he said.

As young people move from adolescence into adulthood, they need services and support that help them build strong foundations and become contributing citizens.

Dr Jat said addressing the challenges facing young people requires government ministries and partners to work together.

He congratulated the Government of Fiji and different line ministries for their efforts to comprehensively empower young people.

The Ministry of Health and Medical Services is working to strengthen youth-friendly health services, train healthcare providers and provide services to young people.

UNFPA is also working with the Ministry of Education to provide family life education to students in schools.

For young people who are out of school, similar information is provided through work with the Ministry of Youth and Sports.

The programs reach young people at youth training centres and in villages through youth clubs.

Trained health facilitators from the Ministry of Youth and Sports provide information on reproductive health, decision-making and healthy choices.

Dr Jat also highlighted collaboration with the Ministry of Labour on employment opportunities, as well as work with the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection and the Ministry of Justice on human rights and the prevention and response to gender-based violence.

For young people living in geographically isolated communities, accessing information can be a challenge.

item.title: YOUTH DEVELOPMENT I Stand up and shape Fiji’s future
item.description: THE message to young people in Navosa was direct during the Navosa Youth Festival – the future of their communities and Fiji will be shaped by the choices they make today. item.content:encoded:
THE message to young people in Navosa was direct during the Navosa Youth Festival – the future of their communities and Fiji will be shaped by the choices they make today.

Speaking at the Navosa Youth Festival, the Minister for Youth and Sports challenged young people to take a stronger role in confronting issues affecting their generation, particularly substance abuse, while also promoting education, sport, skills, family, faith and leadership as pathways towards a healthier future.

“You have to decide what kind of future you want,” Mr Saukuru said.

“You have to decide what kind of Navosa and Nadroga you want to live in. And you have to decide what kind of Fiji you want to inherit and eventually lead.”

The speech placed young people at the centre of the response to some of the country’s most pressing social challenges, urging them not to remain bystanders but to become part of the solution.

The Minister called on young people to stand up, organise, speak out and lead.

The challenge came with a warning about the growing exposure of young people to drugs and other substances in the country.

“The exposure of our young generation to drugs and other substances is a serious concern,” the Minister said.

“We cannot normalise it. We cannot look away. We cannot say that it is someone else’s problem. It is your problem. It is our problem.”

The Minister urged young people themselves to play a role in preventing substance abuse and resisting social pressures that could make drug use appear acceptable.

“Say no to a culture that tells you that substance abuse is a pathway to popularity or acceptance,” he said.

Instead, young people were encouraged to make choices that could strengthen their futures.

“Choose sport. Choose education. Choose skills, choose your family. Choose your faith. Choose your future.”

His message extended beyond drugs, recognising that youth development must address several interconnected challenges.

Concerns around HIV and AIDS were also highlighted, with the Minister calling for greater awareness, responsible choices, testing, compassion and an end to stigma.

The speech also placed mental health among the issues requiring more open discussion.

He said some young people were carrying burdens that their families and friends might never see.

“We must speak openly about mental health,” Mr Saukuru said.

“There are young people among us who are struggling silently, some carrying burdens that their families and friends may never see.”

Creating supportive communities, he said, should mean making it easier for young people to ask for help.

“Asking for help is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign of courage,” he said.

Another key part of the message was the need to stand firmly against violence against women and children.

The Minister said there should be no place for violence or abuse in homes, communities, churches, sporting fields or wider society.

The Minister also challenged young men to rethink traditional ideas about strength.

“Our young men must understand that strength is not demonstrated through violence,” he said.

“Strength is demonstrated through respect, responsibility and self-control.”

At the same time, young women were reminded of their right to dignity, safety and opportunity.

“Our young women must know that they deserve to live with dignity, safety, and opportunity,” the Minister said.

The Minister also drew attention to young people and other vulnerable members of communities who are experiencing homelessness, addiction or disconnection from their families and society.

His message called for a change in how communities viewed people facing these difficulties.

item.title: THE CONCERNED CITIZEN I When will the people experience change?
item.description: The cost of living are a burden on many ordinary families. Now concerns over crime are now adding to that unease. What lies ahead remains uncertain. Yet one troubling pattern is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: reports of sacrilege continue to surface all over Fiji, particularly in relation to temples.
item.content:encoded:
The cost of living are a burden on many ordinary families. Now concerns over crime are now adding to that unease.

What lies ahead remains uncertain. Yet one troubling pattern is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: reports of sacrilege continue to surface all over Fiji, particularly in relation to temples.

Fiji recorded more than 18 reported cases of sacrilege in 2021, one is compelled to wonder if there were many others which did not hit the statistics. The emergence of further incidents now compels us to ask a difficult question: are we witnessing a resurgence of such offences?

At least two alleged acts of sacrilege have come to my attention within the past seven days. This inevitably raises the question of why the Fiji Police Force has not communicated more openly about such incidents through its official channels. Is there a rationale for the absence of public communication? Are there investigative sensitivities that the public may not be aware of, or are there other factors affecting how these cases are being communicated and pursued?

These are legitimate questions, and the victims are entitled to clarity and meaningful action. They should not be left to bear these concerns in isolation. Their concerns deserve attention. As a society, we must stand with them, ensure that their voices are heard, and demand that justice is pursued.

Given the resources allocated to the Fiji Police Force, it is difficult not to question whether the issue lies in resources, operational capacity, accountability, or the manner in which those resources are being utilised. The Government has allocated $226.5 million to the Fiji Police Force under the 2026–2027 Budget, compared with $240.3 million in the 2025–2026 Budget. The Police Commissioner has maintained that the reduced allocation will not compromise public safety or the Force’s operations.

Yet I still find it difficult to understand why the public continues to perceive shortcomings in the police response. Somewhere within this equation, there must be an issue that warrants closer examination. Is it a matter of resources, deployment, responsiveness, accountability, or simply the way existing resources are being utilised? The bottom line is that taxpayers are shouldering these costs as an investment in public safety. What the public deserves in return is not merely expenditure, but visible action, accountability and measurable results.

Fiji is a multi-faith nation, yet a troubling number of reports appear to involve Hindu temples. I genuinely hope someone is willing to answer the question of why. I recognise that there have also been reported cases of property damage and acts of sacrilege involving places of worship belonging to other faiths, but the repeated reports involving temples cannot simply be brushed aside. Is this a pattern, or is it merely a coincidence? I continue to wonder.

I have gathered this from reports in the mainstream media as well as posts circulating on social media. But we must also recognise an important distinction: those who write or post on social media may not always have the same access to authorities as mainstream media organisations.

This, in turn, raises another important question: what exactly have authorities done in response to growing concerns over crime and the protection of places of worship? What proactive measures or strategies are in place to monitor, prevent and address such social issues? And can anyone assure the public that there will be no further acts of this nature?

It is profoundly distressing to continue witnessing such incidents, particularly when those affected may feel that their concerns are falling on deaf ears or receiving inadequate attention. For the victims, this is not merely another statistic or another headline. It is their place of worship, their sense of security and, in many cases, a deeply personal and spiritual space that has been violated. To witness such incidents repeatedly is, without question, an excruciatingly difficult experience.

A positive development is that the campaign period for the next general election may hopefully begin very soon. When prospective candidates and political parties go before the people seeking their votes, I have no doubt that there will be a mouthful of promises: reduced expenditure, greater freedom of speech, better security services, less crime and much more. But promises alone cannot be the measure of leadership.

The public should not hesitate to ask the questions that matter—not merely the questions that fit neatly into an election campaign. What is your plan to address crime? What will you do to protect places of worship? And, most importantly, what concrete measures will you put in place rather than simply making promises during an election campaign?

These are questions the public has every right to ask, and candidates should be prepared to answer them. As the cost of living places greater pressure on households, concerns about crime and social hardship also deserve greater attention. Economic hardship does not excuse criminal behaviour, but it is reasonable to ask whether increasing financial pressure is contributing to some forms of offending.

When the Government continues to charge 12.5 percent VAT on taxable goods and services, the question remains whether the relief reaching ordinary people is sufficient when they continue to bear the cost at the point of purchase.

And if parliamentary salaries and other public expenses continue to rise rather than fall, the burden will ultimately remain with the people. The people, after all, are the ones who continue to pay the price. There is also the question of money coming into the country for specific purposes and how clearly its eventual use is communicated to the public.

In May, Australia committed A$30 million in additional budget support to Fiji to help address rising fuel costs and cost-of-living pressures, including support connected to bus fares. Yet ordinary people are entitled to ask: where, in their daily lives, is the tangible benefit of such assistance being felt?

People continue to look at the price of getting from one place to another and ask whether the relief promised on paper is translating into relief in reality. I cross my fingers until my bones hurt that, come September, the bus fare will finally move closer to the $0.75 Stage One adult fare that many ordinary commuters would welcome.

People, regardless of their employment status, continue to bear the cost of consumption taxes. Even children, when making purchases of taxable goods, encounter VAT embedded in the prices they pay. So the question remains: where is all this money going, and where are the tangible improvements that ordinary people can see and feel?

We continue to hear concerns about pressure on health facilities. The Ministry continues to depend on support and donations. Overfilled buses continue to struggle along our roads. Potholes continue to appear. And while the Viria Water Project has already begun supplying water, its existing 40-million-litre-per-day capacity is still being expanded towards the planned 80 million litres per day. My question is, does it really take an additional three and a half years to complete and existing project?

Meanwhile, when citizens need the police, there remain concerns about whether assistance arrives with the urgency expected of a public service entrusted with their safety. At what point do we stop measuring progress by the amount of money allocated and start measuring it by the quality of life that ordinary people actually experience?

If the cost of living continues to place pressure on ordinary families, and if the public continues to see reports of theft, sacrilege and other offences, then we have to ask: Where are we heading?

Krishneel Nair is Fiji citizen and a Sanatani. He contrbutes opinion pieces occasionally to this newpaper. The views expressed in this article are his and do not reflect the views of this newspaper.

item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I Where Tailevu’s memories still live
item.description: FOR years, Tailevu Hotel stood as a familiar landmark in Korovou Town, carrying the character of a colonial-era hotel and serving as a stopping point for travellers passing through Tailevu North. But there was a time when its future appeared uncertain.
item.content:encoded:
FOR years, Tailevu Hotel stood as a familiar landmark in Korovou Town, carrying the character of a colonial-era hotel and serving as a stopping point for travellers passing through Tailevu North.

But there was a time when its future appeared uncertain.

The hotel had lost some of its spark, and many wondered whether the once-famous establishment had reached the end of its story.

Today, that story is taking a different turn.

With years of repairs, renovations and improvements, Tailevu Hotel has reclaimed its place as a popular stopover for visitors to Korovou Town, while also becoming a place where locals can enjoy a meal, have a drink and unwind after a long day.

Tailevu Hotel director Oliver Williams said the journey began with his parents, Warick Williams and Kuila Kaci of Ryda Limited, now known as Ryda Proprietary Limited (RPL).

In 1992, they bought the hotel from Gokal.

The property was run down at the time, Williams said, and the family began working on the building before leasing it to Mr Subash.

Later, they took the property back, repaired damages and continued operating the hotel.

That process of repairing, improving and maintaining the property has continued over the years.

Building back, one improvement at a time

The transformation of Tailevu Hotel did not happen overnight.

It unfolded through a series of improvements that gradually changed the property and helped restore its appeal.

Mains power was eventually supplied to the property, although electricity cuts meant the hotel still needed its generator.

The Niu extension was built between 1998 and 2000, providing the much-needed accommodation area.

More recently, the hotel continued to invest in the property.

A covered walkway to the Niu extension was built in 2020, followed by a new driveway in 2023.

The lounge has also undergone renovations between 2017 and 2026, while a few minor works continue around the hotel.

Each improvement represents another step in the hotel’s long journey from a run-down property to a more welcoming destination.

The changes are not simply about appearance. They reflect an effort to preserve a place with a long history while making it useful and comfortable for today’s visitors.

Walking into the dining area, the hotel’s colonial character is difficult to miss.

Beautiful colonial touches blend with warm wooden tones, giving the room a rustic and welcoming character.

A polished timber floor stretches through the centre of the room, reflecting natural light filtering through large windows dressed in soft white curtains. The ceiling, lined with closely fitted bamboo, adds an unmistakable Fiji character.

Wooden tables and chairs fill the room. Some are covered with crisp white tablecloths, while others feature colourful floral-patterned fabric that brings life to the space.

Framed photographs, artwork and traditional-looking wooden pieces decorate the walls, adding a sense of history and place.

There is an orderly simplicity to the room, but it does not feel formal.

Instead, it has an unhurried atmosphere, a place where timber, soft curtains and colourful table coverings come together to create a setting that feels familiar and distinctly Pacific.

Large windows also connect the dining space with the landscape outside, allowing a gentle breeze from the nearby river to move through the room.

For diners, the setting provides more than a place to eat.

It offers a chance to slow down and take in views towards Korovou Town while enjoying a meal.

item.title: WEDDING BELLS I Shelvin and Arishma – From FB friends to lovers
item.description: A NAME simply spotted on an FNU assignment led to a Facebook friend request, and a friendship that slowly blossomed into love. Thirteen years later, after navigating distance and shared dreams, Shelvin Chand and Arishma Ashwini Kumar stood side by side as husband and wife.
item.content:encoded:
A NAME simply spotted on an FNU assignment led to a Facebook friend request, and a friendship that slowly blossomed into love.

Thirteen years later, after navigating distance and shared dreams, Shelvin Chand and Arishma Ashwini Kumar stood side by side as husband and wife.

For Shelvin and Arishma, their wedding was never the beginning of their love story. It was the next chapter of one they had written together since they first met in person in July 2013.

Shelvin, 33, a welder from Lautoka who now resides in Melbourne, Australia, and Arishma, 33, a trainer and assessor from Navua who also lives in Melbourne, exchanged their wedding vows on July 11, 2026 – a date that had already carried special meaning in their relationship.

Their wedding celebrations stretched across four days, from July 9 to 12, bringing together faith, family, tradition and friends from Fiji and around the world.

But behind the celebrations was a story built not on a single dramatic moment, but on the small acts of care and commitment that accumulated over 13 years.

It started with a name and a friend request

Their story technically began in 2012, when both were studying at FNU. Arishma was in her first year and Shelvin was in his final year.

Shelvin first became curious about Arishma after seeing her name on assignments his cousin Ashneel brought home for referencing.

“I remember wondering who this Arishma was,” Shelvin recalled.

He eventually noticed her around Derrick Campus and found her on Facebook. He sent her a friend request and was pleased when she accepted.

For months, they communicated through Facebook before eventually moving to phone calls. They did not even exchange phone numbers at first.

Shelvin said he quickly noticed that Arishma was straightforward, humble, funny and easy to talk to.

“When we finally met in person, I was nervous but also excited,” he said.

By the time they met face-to-face, they had already spent months talking online, so she felt as though she knew him.

“I remember feeling a little nervous and shy when we finally met but there was something very comfortable and natural about being around him,” she said.

Their first meeting was not a grand romantic occasion. In July 2013, near FNU’s Derrick Campus in Samabula, they finally met in person and walked home together.

Shelvin was living in Cunningham while Arishma was living at Centrepoint.

There was no elaborate date or romantic setup, just two friends finally meeting after months of conversations behind a screen.

Neither expected that the friendship would eventually lead to marriage.

Arishma had previously experienced a major heartbreak and had prayed that the next person who entered her life would be someone who genuinely loved her, accepted her and would walk through life with her.

When Shelvin arrived, she did not immediately recognise him as the answer to that prayer.

“There wasn’t a dramatic ‘love at first sight’ moment,” she said.

Instead, the relationship grew naturally.

They spent time together, continued talking and allowed their friendship to develop without pressure or expectations.

Some of their earliest memories remain among their most meaningful.

One came during Arishma’s final exams at FNU. She and her friends were spending long hours studying at the Derrick Campus library and surviving on mince loaf from the French Bakery across the road.

Shelvin knew she was not eating properly.

One day, he made her a chicken sandwich and brought it to her.

“It sounds like such a small thing, but I remember eating that sandwich and feeling so genuinely cared for,” Arishma said.

item.title: FOCUS I What is parentification?
item.description: Eve was an adult when she realised she grew up in a home where child-parent roles were reversed. Eve and her siblings were in school when they began taking on adult responsibilities at home, due to their mother’s declining mental health.
item.content:encoded:
Eve was an adult when she realised she grew up in a home where child-parent roles were reversed.

Eve and her siblings were in school when they began taking on adult responsibilities at home, due to their mother’s declining mental health.

The now-51-year-old from Sydney/Gadigal lands recalls her mother spending most days in bed due to severe depression and her father becoming increasingly absent.

“Mum would leave instructions for getting dinner ready and she’d leave the stuff in the fridge,” says Eve, not her real name.

“Then as time went on, we were basically running the household, doing everything from cooking, laundry, cleaning, shopping, all of that.”

As well as doing physical labour, Eve, who was a young teenager when she first took on these responsibilities, says she also became an emotional support for her mother, who had experienced childhood sexual trauma.

“Mum would talk to me about what had happened to her [as a child] and she was basically using me as kind of like a quasi-counsellor, it was really inappropriate.”

Eve says at the time she wasn’t able to process what was happening, she just “got on with it”.

It wasn’t until she studied to become a social worker that she came across the term parentification and finally “felt validated”.

Parentification is a psychological term used to describe a role reversal where children have parental-level responsibilities above what is deemed developmentally appropriate, according to Rachael Sharman, a lecturer and researcher in psychology, specialising in child/adolescent development.

She says people can experience different forms of parentification and at varying degrees of severity.

“I used to work in child protection, and this was something that we looked out for quite a lot,” says Sharman, based on the Sunshine Coast/Kabi Kabi lands.

“[One day] we were talking to a mother, we noticed her six-year-old daughter come home from school, jump up to the kitchen bench, get herself something to eat and drink, then proceeded to wipe down all the benches and table, make the baby a bottle and feed the baby.”

Children who are parentified take on emotional and instrumental responsibilities before their brain is developmentally ready, but also before they are ready emotionally, according to Deirdre Brandner, a child and adolescent psychologist, based in Melbourne/Naarm.

But she believes emotional parentification is more damaging, because the child is managing the emotions of the parents.

“This is when kids are the parents’ confidant or they’re the emotional regulator for the parents, [for example] ‘Dad looks like he’s stressed, I need to go and do this to make sure he’s OK.’”

Brander says international studies, including a large, nationally representative study from Poland in 2021, suggest “up to one in three young people, particularly adolescents” experience emotional parentification.

But she says the signs of parentification in children are often “subtle because people see these kids as mature, as helpful, as capable, as highly competent”.

Hyper vigilance to other people’s moods, even peers at school

Feeling responsible for adults’ wellbeing

Sharman says “it can manifest quite differently” depending on the age of the person and the severity of the parentification.

“What we typically see is around the age of 16 to 25, that later adolescence, they start to work out that something’s not right.”

A life of ‘hyper independence and responsibility’

As an adult, Eve says she has found it difficult to say no to extra responsibilities, put her own needs first, while being hyper independent.

“I’ve never had that experience of parents turning up to stuff, going on a university tour with me when I was at the end of year 12, or getting my driver’s licence,” she says.

She also found herself in an intimate relationship that mirrored the unhealthy family dynamic she grew up with.

“Even though [ending that relationship] has been incredibly difficult, I can look back on that now and understand why I went into it,” she says.

But there were some positives. Eve says she is a more “compassionate and empathetic person” and credits her successful 20-year career in the public mental health sector to her childhood experiences.

Children who are parentified take on emotional and instrumental responsibilities before their brain is developmentally ready. Picture: www.childfocusnj.org

item.title: BEHIND THE NEWS I An alliance of equals
item.description: When Fiji signed the Ocean of Peace Alliance with Australia last month, it crossed a historic threshold. For the first time since independence, Fiji entered a formal mutual defence treaty which commits both nations to come to each other’s aid in times of greatest need. It is, by any measure, a landmark agreement. The treaty elevates the Vuvale relationship beyond development assistance and militar
item.content:encoded:
When Fiji signed the Ocean of Peace Alliance with Australia last month, it crossed a historic threshold. For the first time since independence, Fiji entered a formal mutual defence treaty which commits both nations to come to each other’s aid in times of greatest need.

It is, by any measure, a landmark agreement. The treaty elevates the Vuvale relationship beyond development assistance and military cooperation into something far more consequential: a reciprocal security commitment. Australia describes it as one of its formal alliances, while Fiji presents it as a partnership built on shared sovereignty and regional stability. The language is reassuring, the symbolism powerful. But behind the ceremony lies a serious question that deserves public discussion.

If Australia were attacked tomorrow, what exactly could Fiji contribute?

This is not a question of loyalty. It is a question of capability.

Mutual defence treaties carry enormous political weight because they imply reciprocal obligations. The Australia–Fiji agreement states that both countries will come to one another’s assistance during their “times of greatest need”, reflecting the collective defence principle found in many military alliances around the world.

Yet reciprocity between unequal partners has always been complicated.

Australia possesses one of the Indo-Pacific’s most capable militaries: blue-water naval vessels, fighter aircraft, submarines, cyber capabilities and sophisticated intelligence networks. Its defence budget runs into tens of billions of dollars annually. Fiji’s Republic of Fiji Military Forces (RFMF), by contrast, has traditionally been structured around territorial security, peacekeeping and humanitarian response rather than conventional warfare.

The imbalance is obvious. An attack on Fiji would likely see Australia providing ships, aircraft, logistics, surveillance and intelligence almost immediately. But if Australia faced a comparable threat, Fiji cannot realistically offer equivalent military power.

That does not make the treaty meaningless. It simply raises the question of what reciprocity actually looks like.

International treaties often treat states as juridically equal regardless of their size. A country of one million people signs alongside a nation of 27 million with equal sovereign status. Legally, that principle is important.

Operationally, however, equality becomes more nuanced.

Consider the hypothetical scenario that has lingered quietly since the treaty was announced. Australia comes under military attack. Its northern approaches are contested. Maritime supply routes require protection. Would Fiji dispatch troops? Patrol vessels? Engineers? Medical teams? Intelligence officers? Or would its contribution be largely symbolic — a political declaration of support alongside specialised assistance where possible?

The treaty does not erase the reality that Fiji’s armed forces were never designed to fight Australia’s wars.

There is another way of viewing security altogether.

For decades, Fiji has earned international respect not because of overwhelming military strength, but because of disciplined peacekeepers. From the Middle East to Africa, Fijian soldiers have built a reputation for professionalism under United Nations mandates. Disaster response has become another defining strength, with the RFMF regularly deployed during cyclones, floods and regional emergencies.

Modern security is increasingly multidimensional. Cybersecurity, humanitarian assistance, maritime surveillance, illegal fishing, disaster logistics and infrastructure resilience are now as strategically important as tanks and missiles. Australia’s engagement with Pacific countries has increasingly focused on these areas rather than preparing island states for conventional interstate warfare.

If that is the true intention of the alliance, then public expectations should reflect it.

Because when ordinary citizens hear the phrase “mutual defence”, many understandably imagine soldiers defending each other’s territory in battle. The practical reality may be far broader — and far less dramatic.

The treaty also arrives during a period of intensifying geopolitical competition.

Australia has been strengthening defence partnerships across the Pacific, including agreements with Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and now Fiji, as strategic rivalry between major powers becomes increasingly pronounced.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has consistently argued that Fiji’s foreign policy remains one of friendship with all and enemies with none. The Ocean of Peace concept itself seeks to place Pacific priorities — not great-power rivalry — at the centre of regional security.

That aspiration is admirable. But bilateral defence alliances inevitably create perceptions. Whether intended or not, they are interpreted by larger powers as strategic alignment.

For Fiji, the challenge is maintaining strategic autonomy while benefiting from closer security cooperation. The stronger the alliance becomes, the more important it is for Suva to clearly articulate where its obligations begin and where they end.

None of this is an argument against the treaty.

Australia has long been Fiji’s closest security partner. The two countries cooperate extensively on maritime surveillance, military training, humanitarian response and peacekeeping. Formalising that relationship may well enhance regional stability and improve Fiji’s own preparedness for natural disasters and emerging security threats.

But democratic oversight requires asking difficult questions before a crisis, not during one.

What constitutes an “attack” that triggers mutual assistance?

Is military deployment automatic, or does each Parliament retain discretion?

What forms of assistance satisfy Fiji’s obligations — combat forces, logistics, intelligence or humanitarian support?

Would Fiji be expected to contribute beyond the Pacific if Australia were involved in a wider regional conflict?

item.title: YOUTH I Youths connect to celebrate
item.description: YOUNG people from across Navosa were given a platform to connect and celebrate as the Navosa Youth Festival brought together sport, entertainment, information and community engagement. The festival formed part of Fiji’s national celebration of International Youth Day and included booths where organisations and businesses shared information and services with young people from the province.
item.content:encoded:
YOUNG people from across Navosa were given a platform to connect and celebrate as the Navosa Youth Festival brought together sport, entertainment, information and community engagement.

The festival formed part of Fiji’s national celebration of International Youth Day and included booths where organisations and businesses shared information and services with young people from the province.

Rugby matches, entertainment and other activities added to the celebrations, creating a space where young people could take part, discover opportunities and connect with organisations working in their communities.

During the celebration, Youth and Sports Minister Jese Saukuru officially handed over gym equipment to Navosa Central College, which will also be used by the Navosa Rugby Union.

For Mr Saukuru, the festival represented more than a day of activities.

“This is your day, this is your platform and this is your opportunity,” he told young people from Navosa and Nadroga.

Different backgrounds, shared aspirations

International Youth Day is observed globally on August 12 each year.

This year’s theme, “Different Contexts Common Aspirations”, reflects the different experiences of young people while recognising the aspirations they share.

Saukuru said young people came from different islands, villages, schools, communities, cultures and backgrounds. They also faced different challenges.

But beneath those differences were common hopes and dreams.

“They want dignity, they want opportunities, they want quality educational skills, they want decent employment and meaningful livelihoods,” he said.

Young people also wanted to participate in decisions affecting their lives, to be healthy, safe and respected, and to be heard.

For the Minister, young people should not be viewed only as future leaders.

He acknowledged the contribution young Fijians were already making in rural and maritime communities, towns and cities, schools, workplaces, sporting fields and youth clubs.

“We see young people stepping forward and lead community activities, we see young people learning new skills, we see them taking part in sport, we see young entrepreneurs creating opportunities for themselves and others and we see young people speaking up on issues that matter to their communities,” he said.

Although individual contributions could sometimes appear small, Saukuru said they made a difference when brought together.

“Our young people are not just the leaders of tomorrow, you are leaders and contributors today,” he said.

That belief sits at the centre of the Ministry of Youth and Sports’ approach, with youth development and sports development serving as two important ways of reaching young people.

Saukuru said youth development was about more than organising programs.

“It is about creating pathways. It is about building confidence; it is about developing leadership. It is about giving young people skills, knowledge, values, and opportunities.”

Sport, he said, also carried lessons beyond competition.

“It teaches discipline, it teaches teamwork, it teaches resilience, it teaches respect, it teaches young people how to win with humility and how to lose with dignity.”

The Navosa Youth Festival was also a fulfilment of a request made during Saukuru’s visit to Nukuilau Village.

During that visit, he was asked whether a youth festival could be held in Navosa.

“My answer was a simple yes and today, we are here,” he said.

The festival turned that conversation into an event bringing young people together through sports, cultural activities, skills training, exhibitions and community activities.

For Saukuru, such festivals provide spaces where young people can feel valued and discover their talents, while communities can begin conversations about difficult issues affecting them.

“These festivals are much more than sporting competitions,” he said.

They bring together sport, culture, leadership, awareness, community engagement and conversations around issues affecting young people.
